name: Edaganathar Temple, Thiruvedagam
deity: Shiva as Edaganathar, with the goddess Elavarkuzhali
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Pandya Nadu on the Vaigai, sung by Sambandar in the Tevaram (7th century); present structure of the Nayak period
dynasty: Pandya origins; rebuilt in the Nayak period, with Vijayanagara-era records
summary: On the Vaigai near Sholavandan, Shiva is worshipped as Edaganathar, Lord of the palm leaf, where tradition says Sambandar's hymn, cast on the river, swam upstream against the current and came to rest.

sections.history: Thiruvedagam is a village on the Vaigai about 18 km north-west of Madurai, close to Sholavandan, and its temple is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams of the Tevaram, counted among the fourteen of Pandya Nadu. Thirugnana Sambandar sang its Lord, and the shrine is bound up with the most dramatic chapter of his life: his visit to Madurai in the seventh century, at the call of the Pandya queen Mangaiyarkkarasi and the minister Kulachirai, to win the king back to the worship of Shiva. The first temple is attributed to the Pandyas; the present stone structure belongs largely to the Nayak period, and inscriptions of the later Pandya and Vijayanagara eras are recorded here.
sections.architecture: The temple has two gateway towers, one leading to the sanctum of Edaganathar and one to the shrine of the goddess Elavarkuzhali, so that each has its own approach. The halls and enclosures are largely of the Nayak age. Within stands the shrine of Vaadhu Venra Vinayagar, the Ganesha who won the debate, closely tied to the temple's story. The sacred tank is the Brahma Theertham, the sacred tree is the vilvam, and the Vaigai flows close by.
sections.legends: When Sambandar met the scholars who opposed him at the Pandya court, tradition tells, the contest was settled by trials. In the trial by water, each side's verses were written on palm leaves and cast into the Vaigai. The others' leaves drifted away with the stream, but Sambandar's leaf turned and moved against the current, coming to rest at this spot — hence the name, from edu, the palm leaf. The minister Kulachirai, following it, found a lingam where it stopped. Temple tradition adds that Vinayagar, in the form of a fish, held the leaf in place.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva festivals of the year — monthly Pradosham, Maha Shivaratri, Arudra Darshanam and the Navaratri days of the goddess — and the story of the floating leaf is retold to pilgrims through the year. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Stand at the riverside and imagine a single palm leaf turning against the current of the Vaigai: that is the story Thiruvedagam keeps. Worship Edaganathar and the goddess at their two shrines, greet the Vinayagar of the debate, and pair the visit with Madurai, where the rest of Sambandar's Pandya story unfolds.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most village temples around Madurai. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer areas, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruvedagam is about 18 km north-west of Madurai on the road to Sholavandan, and about 3 km from Sholavandan, which has the nearest railway station; buses run along this route from Madurai. Madurai Junction is the nearest major railhead, and Madurai Airport the nearest airport.
